newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: SLOVAK POLICE SHELVE KIDNAPPING-RELATED PROBES.
newsitem.headline: SLOVAK POLICE SHELVE KIDNAPPING-RELATED PROBES.

text.p: Slovak police have shelved two further cases connected to the abduction of the son of President Michal Kovac, the Interior Ministry said on Tuesday.
Two almost identical statements issued on both cases said that they had both been adjourned for lack of evidence which would have enabled police to make further progress.
Last year's kidnapping of Michal Kovac Junior to Austria provoked uproar, with the opposition linking it with a bitter feud between the president and Prime Minister Vladimir Meciar.

One case was the investigation of the origin and authenticity of an recording of a telephone conversation allegedly between former interior minister Ludovit Hudek and Ivan Lexa, the head of the SIS secret service, on sacking an investigator probing the kidnapping.
The second investigation is into the death of Robert Remias, whose car exploded in Bratislava last April.
Remias was a close friend and contact of former SIS officer Oskar Fegyveres who said he had taken part in the kidnapping which had been organised and carried on the orders of Lexa.
Two investigators were removed from the kidnapping case after indicating they had evidence implicating the SIS. A third adjourned the probe last May, also citing lack of evidence.
Kovak Junior was seized near Bratislava on August 31, 1995, bundled into the boot of his car and dumped outside a police station 10 km (six miles) inside neigbouring Austria.
He was detained in Austria to face extradition to Germany on suspicion of fraud but a Vienna court later freed him.

Two veteran detectives were taken off the case and later quit the police after their investigations led them to ask Lexa for permission to question SIS officers alleged by Fegyveres to have taken part in the kidnappping.
Fegyveres went into hiding abroad and Remias, a former police officer, remained his only contact.

Remias was killed last April when his car mysteriously blew up on the outskirts o Bratislava. At first police said the explosion was caused by a gas leak but later said it appeared had been caused by an explosive device.

An unofficial commission investigating the kidnapping headed by Ladislav Pittner, a former interior minister and member of the opposition Christian Democratic Movement (KDH), has accused Hudek and Lexa of complicity in the kidnapping and the subsequent cover-up.
Lexa and Hudek, both close collaborators of Meciar, have denied any complicity.
Last August Hudek was sacked in a government reshuffle and replaced by Gustav Krajcik, a former senior official of Meciar's ruling Movement for a Democratic Slovakia (HZDS).
If proved authentic the tape of the conversation between Hudek and Lexa would present concrete evidence of the involvement of the Interior Ministry and SIS in the kidnapping.

The opposition alleges that the kidnapping was engineered to compromise President Kovac. The president was instrumental in Meciar's dismissal as premier in the spring of 1994 by calling on parliament to pass a non-confidence vote.

Meciar bounced back in the autumn of that year and has since whittled away the president's powers and several times called for his resignation. But he lacks the necessary three fifths parliamentary majority to vote Kovac out of office.
